chapter: Later ventures, lodges and San Francisco recollections
title: The store as hiring hall, booking office and film extras source
summary: Musicians and entertainers hung around the store; studios called for bands and Black extras, until a man upstairs took over the booking and moved to Central Casting.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: I see. I read several times in several places that your store evolved into kind of a hiring hall or almost booking agency...

Well, they...they...all of the musicians and entertainers used to kind of hang around out there, you know, and... because, you know, sometime we'd have a job...Well, we'd get calls for four or five bands in a night, and then we'd have to hustle up bands for the rest of the engagement. And then the...Warner Bros. and all of them used to call us for the Negro entertainers, you know, and Negro mu...par... you know, actors and things.

Oh, yeah, they used to call us. They...now in those days, they's making a lot of African pictures, you know--runnin' around with G-cloths and things had on, and, like "The Klansman" and all those pictures they made, so they'd call back there, and sometime we'd send fifty or a hundred out there at a time, you know. Just

atmospheres, you know. Atmospheric people, like there'd be African picture, and they'd have a lot of Africans out there and things like that, so it was...it was kind of a headquarters, you know, for anything they wanted, they'd call the Spikes Brothers, and they could sent it out there. Find it--we'd find it and get it.
So people looking for jobs would hang around the store on the chance that you might get a call...

Well, had...knew pretty well who to call, you know, and then eventually, they was a fellow that opened up--upstairs over us--he opened up his own office of...of...booking, and then he took all that over, and then, eventually, they...he had so much of it that they called him and gave him a job in the uh...uh, Central Casting, and he handled all the Negro business.

I can't think of his name. It's too way far back. He stayed out there for a long time--ten or twelve years--till I think he got too old or something. And that's the job they wanted to give me, and I wouldn't take it because he, after I closed the music store, I told you, I made this picture for this Chinee picture, and the man that made the Chinee picture wanted me to...uh, go and take a job over there. But this boy had the job, and I wouldn't run under him, you know.
